title: ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may God be pleased with him)
subtitle: al-Fārūq, the second Rightly Guided Caliph

name.label: Full name
name.value: ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb ibn Nufayl ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā ibn Riyāḥ ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Qurṭ ibn Razāḥ ibn ʿAdī ibn Kaʿb ibn Luʾayy al-Qurashī al-ʿAdawī

kunya.label: Kunya and title
kunya.value: Abū Ḥafṣ; his epithet is al-Fārūq

birth.label: Birth
birth.value: In Makkah, about thirteen years after the Year of the Elephant according to some reports

death.label: Death
death.value: Dhū al-Ḥijja 23 AH (644 CE), in Madinah

burial.label: Burial
burial.value: In the chamber of ʿĀʾisha, beside the Prophet ﷺ and Abū Bakr

claims.identity.lineage: ʿUmar belonged to the Quraysh, from the clan of Banū ʿAdī ibn Kaʿb; his lineage meets that of the Prophet ﷺ at Kaʿb ibn Luʾayy.
claims.identity.names: His kunya, Abū Ḥafṣ, refers to his daughter Ḥafṣa; his epithet is al-Fārūq.
claims.identity.mother: Most reports name his mother as Ḥantama bint Hāshim ibn al-Mughīra of the Makhzūm; other reports say she was the daughter of Hishām ibn al-Mughīra. Genealogists differ on her father’s name.
claims.identity.amir: He was the first to be called “Amīr al-Muʾminīn” (Commander of the Believers) in Islam.
claims.early.birth: He was born in Makkah about thirteen years after the Year of the Elephant according to some reports; the reports differ on the exact year of his birth.
claims.early.clan: He grew up among the Banū ʿAdī, a clan of standing in Quraysh, whose responsibility included acting as envoys between Quraysh and others.
claims.early.work: Some reports mention that in his youth he tended camels for his father; these reports have not yet been reviewed.
claims.conv.islam: ʿUmar accepted Islam in Makkah after having strongly opposed the new message, and became one of the most prominent Muslims.
claims.conv.date: Most reports place his conversion in the sixth year of the mission, after that of Ḥamza; other reports differ on the year.
claims.conv.story: The biographical tradition tells that he accepted Islam after visiting his sister Fāṭima and her husband Saʿīd ibn Zayd and reading a page containing Sūrat Ṭā-Hā; the reports differ in their details and in how firmly hadith scholars consider them established.
claims.proph.closeness: ʿUmar was among the closest Companions of the Prophet ﷺ, and his name is often mentioned together with Abū Bakr’s in accounts of companionship and counsel.
claims.proph.hafsa: The Prophet ﷺ married Ḥafṣa bint ʿUmar, so ʿUmar became the Prophet’s father-in-law.
claims.proph.battles: He took part with the Prophet ﷺ in Badr, Uḥud, the Trench, the Conquest of Makkah and the other campaigns.
claims.proph.hudaybiyyah: At the Treaty of al-Ḥudaybiya, ʿUmar questioned the Prophet ﷺ about the terms of the treaty; he is later reported to have performed good deeds because of this.
claims.proph.death: When the Prophet ﷺ died, ʿUmar at first denied that he had died, then calmed down when Abū Bakr addressed the people and recited a verse from Sūrat Āl ʿImrān.
claims.events.hijra: ʿUmar emigrated to Madinah before the Prophet ﷺ, as part of a group of emigrants.
claims.events.badr: At Badr, ʿUmar advised putting the prisoners to death while Abū Bakr advised accepting ransom; revelation then came concerning the prisoners.
claims.comp.abubakr: ʿUmar pledged allegiance to Abū Bakr at the Saqīfa and was among his closest aides; Abū Bakr later designated him as his successor.
claims.comp.khalid: After becoming caliph, ʿUmar removed Khālid ibn al-Walīd from the command of the army in al-Shām; reports and opinions differ on the reasons.
claims.comp.shura: After he was stabbed, ʿUmar left the choice of successor to a council of six: ʿUthmān, ʿAlī, Ṭalḥa, al-Zubayr, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf and Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ.
claims.cal.start: He became caliph in 13 AH (634 CE) after the death of Abū Bakr, and his caliphate lasted about ten years.
claims.cal.conquests: During his rule the conquests extended to al-Shām, Iraq, Egypt and parts of Persia.
claims.cal.jerusalem: He concluded a treaty with the people of Aelia (Jerusalem) and travelled there to receive the city.
claims.cal.admin: He organised the registers (dīwāns) and fixed stipends for the fighters, founded garrison cities such as Basra and Kufa, and appointed and held governors to account.
claims.cal.calendar: The start of dating by the Hijra is attributed to him; reports differ on the year in which this happened and on the details of the consultation.
claims.cal.taraweeh: He gathered the people in Ramadan behind a single imam in the mosque for the tarāwīḥ prayer: Ubayy ibn Kaʿb.
claims.death.attack: He was stabbed by Abū Luʾluʾa (Fīrūz), a Persian slave of al-Mughīra ibn Shuʿba, while leading the dawn prayer in the Prophet’s Mosque.
claims.death.date: This took place at the end of Dhū al-Ḥijja 23 AH (644 CE); reports differ on the exact day and on how many days he lived after the attack.
claims.death.age: Reports differ on his age at death; many narrators give about sixty-three years.
claims.death.burial: He asked ʿĀʾisha’s permission to be buried beside the Prophet ﷺ and Abū Bakr; she granted it, and he was buried in her chamber.
claims.leg.second: He is counted as the second of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, and hadith scholars and historians devote dedicated chapters to his merits and accounts.
claims.leg.justice: In Islamic memory he remains a proverbial example of justice and of holding governors accountable.

birth.label: Birth
birth.when: About 13 years after the Year of the Elephant (some reports)
